opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Darnell. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group that studies how people see changes at work, and nothing you tell me will be linked to your name.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yeah, that's cool. I don't really know nothing about AI though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I don't really care. That's a phone thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Doesn't mean nothing for me. I just gotta keep this job. My grandma's on me about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Show up more, I guess. Get to site on time. Try and get my forklift licence so I make more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Not thinking about it.

S0.say: I don't really care. That's a phone thing.
S0.think: Doesn't mean anything for me. I just need to keep this job.
S0.do: Tries to get to site on time and works toward a forklift licence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing. I wouldn't really talk about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fewer beginners, that's me, right? If they hire less new guys and I'm late a lot, that's bad for me. But they always need guys to carry stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Try not to miss days. For real this time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kind of a little worried. Not much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said 'show up more' twice now. What gets in the way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stuff. The bus. Sometimes I'm just tired. Stuff at home. I know I gotta fix it.

S1.say: Nothing. I wouldn't really talk about it.
S1.think: Fewer new hires and me being late a lot is bad. But they always need guys to carry stuff.
S1.do: Tries not to miss days, for real this time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's crazy for them office people. But that's not my world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Doesn't touch me. I don't work at a desk. Maybe office people know how it feels now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same. Keep working. Maybe ask about them new AI jobs, but I didn't finish school, so probably not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, I guess.

S2.say: That's crazy for the office people. But it's not my world.
S2.think: It doesn't touch me. I don't work at a desk.
S2.do: Keeps working and wonders about the new AI jobs, though he doubts they'd take him without school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say finally guys like me win one. Nah, I'm playing. It's messed up for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Physical stuff is safe, so I'm good? But if all them office people need work, they might come on site. They'd show up on time. That's a problem for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Actually be on time. Ask the foreman what I gotta do to keep my spot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Little nervous.

S3.say: Finally guys like me win one. Nah, it's messed up for them.
S3.think: Physical work is safe, but office people might come on site, and they'd show up on time.
S3.do: Gets to work on time and asks the foreman what he needs to do to keep his spot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say they can't just take all the jobs. What are people supposed to do? That's not right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carrying stuff, cleaning up the site, that's like the first thing a robot does. That's my whole job. I didn't finish school. I don't have nothing else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, for real. Ask my grandma what to do. Try to get any job before the robots come, a store or something. Look for one of them programmes where they pay you to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Like, really scared. Like I'm stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't follow AI news. Is this the first time you've thought about robots on sites?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, pretty much. And now I can't stop thinking about it.

S4.say: They can't just take all the jobs. What are people supposed to do?
S4.think: Carrying and cleaning up is the first thing a robot does. That's my whole job, and I've got nothing else.
S4.do: Asks his grandmother for advice, looks for any store job before robots arrive, and searches for paid training.
